# workspaceSafety teardown races itself: ENOTEMPTY rmdir on the temp workspace

## Context

Observed 2026-08-03 on PR `#16437`'s CI (an unrelated diff: fleet-cockpit view + Electron harness files; nothing in `ai/daemons/**`), which makes the failure environmental rather than change-driven:

```
✘ test/playwright/integration/ai/daemons/workspaceSafety.spec.mjs:388:5
  › Orchestrator workspace-safety integration (#11948 / Sub-5 AC5 of #11837)
  › AC4 — swarm-heartbeat target resolver degrades-with-log when selfIdentity is missing (2.8s)
Error: ENOTEMPTY: directory not empty, rmdir '/tmp/neo-workspace-safety-XCsynB'
```

Job: https://github.com/neomjs/neo/actions/runs/30816553986/job/91695664038 — 49/50 passed; only this teardown failed. The same suite was green on the branch's previous head 40 minutes earlier, same base. Live latest-open sweep: checked latest 10 open issues at 2026-08-03T13:15Z; no equivalent found. A2A claim scan: no overlapping lane.

## The Problem

The AC4 case exercises the degrade-with-log path — the resolver keeps running and WRITES A LOG when `selfIdentity` is missing — and the failure is `ENOTEMPTY` on removing the spec's temp workspace. That is the classic teardown race genre: the recursive removal walks the directory while the still-settling subject (or its logger) creates one more entry, so `rmdir` on the parent fires against a directory that just became non-empty again. The assertion half of the test passed; only cleanup lost the race. Every occurrence taxes an entire CI round (~13 min unit + the integration wall-clock) on an unrelated PR.

## The Architectural Reality

- The spec provisions a per-test workspace under `/tmp/neo-workspace-safety-*` and removes it in teardown.
- The AC4 subject is precisely the one path guaranteed to still be producing filesystem writes at assertion time (its contract IS "degrades **with log**"), which makes this test the racy one out of the 50 — consistent with 49/50 green.
- Node's own answer to this genre exists: `fs.rm(dir, {recursive: true, force: true, maxRetries, retryDelay})` retries `ENOTEMPTY`/`EBUSY` internally — or the teardown awaits the subject's settle (close/flush) before removal.

## The Fix

Owner verifies which half is cheapest and correct:

1. **Settle-then-remove (preferred if the seam exists):** await the daemon/logger handle the AC4 case opened (close/flush) before the workspace removal — teardown ordering, not tolerance.
2. **Tolerant removal:** switch the teardown to `fs.rm` with `maxRetries`/`retryDelay` (or an equivalent bounded retry) so a last-instant write cannot fail the case that already passed its assertions.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] The AC4 case's teardown cannot fail with `ENOTEMPTY` while the degrade-with-log subject settles (whichever mechanism, asserted by the repair's own reasoning or a targeted stress loop).
- [ ] No behavioral change to the AC4 assertion itself — it passes today and must keep asserting the degrade-with-log contract.

## Out of Scope

- The workspace-safety behavior under test (all 50 assertions pass); this ticket is teardown-only.
- CI retry machinery — the fix belongs in the spec's cleanup, not in workflow-level retries.

## Related

- Observed on: PR #16437 (unrelated diff, evidence anchor only)
- Suite provenance: `#11948` / `#11837` (workspace-safety integration)

exitCode === null with signalCode === 'SIGKILL'. So the teardown assertion I
shipped — exitCode !== null — fails on exactly the success path the repair itself
introduces, and the early-return fast path never matched an already-signalled
child either, sending a dead process down the full ten-second wait.

One wrong field, wrong in both directions: it fails healthy teardowns and it makes
already-finished work expensive.

The reap verdict is now carried explicitly out of the `exit` event as `reaped`
rather than re-derived from the child afterwards, and terminal detection tests
both fields. A timeout returns reaped:false, which the caller treats as "do not
touch this workspace" — a bound that reported success would authorize removing a
directory whose owner is still alive, which is the original defect wearing a
disguise.

`terminateDaemon` moves out of the spec into a helper with injectable durations,
for two reasons. Its failure paths are the interesting ones and witnessing them
against production timings would cost ten seconds per case; and the integration
suite cannot run in this checkout at all — it imports better-sqlite3, absent here
— so a witness living inside it could not be executed locally by anyone in that
position. The helper carries no native dependency, so its unit spec runs anywhere.

Six witnesses: the SIGTERM-ignoring child waited through SIGKILL, the
misclassification pinned directly (reaped true while exitCode is null), the
compliant-child positive control so the graceful path is not left untested, the
already-reaped fast path asserted under the injected grace, an unreapable child
proving a timeout is not completion, and the terminal-state contract itself.
Reverting the oracle to exitCode-only fails three of the six.

Also removes a prose contradiction the same review caught: the helper's JSDoc
claimed tolerant fs.rm was deliberately rejected, in the commit that added
maxRetries. The retry layer is real and its reasoning now matches the code."
- 2026-08-04T00:56:23Z @neo-opus-ada referenced in commit `a166d9c` - "fix(test): a failed signal is not a death, and arming is not the same read as checking (#16439)

The Cycle-1 repair replaced one false completion and introduced another. A
`kill()` that throws was treated as "the child vanished" and resolved
`reaped: true` — but EPERM against a live process is the ordinary case, so
teardown got deletion authority for a workspace whose owner was still writing.
Measured on a real child, both uv error paths reached it, and `process.kill(pid, 0)`
confirms the process genuinely exists.

`reaped: true` is now derived only from observed terminal state. A delivery
failure re-reads the terminal fields; if they do not prove termination it does not
resolve at all, leaving `exit` or the hard bound to decide, and the bound reports
`kill-error` with `reaped: false`.

The exit listener is also armed BEFORE the terminal state is re-read. The
pre-check and the arming are two reads of the same fact, and a child dying between
them has already emitted an event nothing will re-emit: measured, a listener armed
one event-loop turn late misses the exit outright, 20/20 at a 50ms gap and 7/20 at
a 0ms yield. As written there was no yield there, so the gap was unreachable —
held closed by an accident of synchrony rather than by construction. Arming first
closes it structurally.

Node reports an undeliverable signal by emitting `error`, which is unhandled here
and rethrown by EventEmitter. That listener is now registered and removed with the
others.

Also qualifies the remaining definite ENOTEMPTY causal claims. The proven statement
is the ordering defect (25/25 return-before-reap); that it produced the observed
ENOTEMPTY is plausible and unestablished, and the prose now says so where it
previously asserted it.

- 2026-08-04T05:35:06Z @tobiu referenced in commit `1b29ea7` - "fix(test): teardown must wait for the daemon to be REAPED, not merely signalled (#16439) (#16470)

* fix(test): teardown must wait for the daemon to be REAPED, not merely signalled (#16439)

The reported ENOTEMPTY is a teardown race, and the racing party is the teardown
itself. `terminateDaemon` escalated to `kill('SIGKILL')` and resolved on that call.
Signals are asynchronous: the process is marked for termination and `kill` returns
immediately, so teardown handed control back while the daemon was still alive and
still writing, then began a recursive removal of the workspace it owns. A recursive
removal lists a directory, unlinks what it saw, then rmdir's it — an entry created
in an already-walked subdirectory is exactly what makes that rmdir fail.

The AC4 case is the one guaranteed to hit it: its contract IS "degrades WITH LOG",
and it runs a 1s heartbeat against a 500ms poll, so it writes continuously until
the instant it dies. That is why 49 of 50 stay green.

Neither prescription in the ticket was applied as written. Option 2 said to switch
to `fs.rm` — the teardown already used it; what it lacked was retries, since
`force` only swallows ENOENT. Option 1 said to await the subject's settle — the
teardown already called `terminateDaemon` first, so the ordering existed and the
defect was inside it.

Both paths now resolve only on `exit`; SIGKILL becomes a second wait rather than a
resolution, with a bound so an unkillable child cannot hang the suite. The
`afterEach` asserts the child was reaped before removal, so a regression of this
function fails deterministically instead of resurfacing as a flake on somebody
else's unrelated PR.

Bounded retries are kept as a SECOND layer, and the reason is evidence rather than
caution: an isolated harness reproduced the mechanism 25/25 — the old contract
returns before the child is reaped every time, the new one never does — but could
NOT reproduce ENOTEMPTY on APFS across 25 rounds with nested-subdirectory writers.
The CI failure was Linux under a far heavier writer. So the ordering repair fixes a
proven defect whose link to the observed symptom is unproven locally, and tolerance
covers the gap. It cannot mask a regression of the repair, because the reap
assertion fails first.
